content.text: Urban areas can be up to 7°C warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb sunlight during the day and release heat at night.

Dr. Helen Carter, a climate scientist, measured temperatures across London using sensors fixed to buses. Her results showed that the hottest areas were those with the fewest trees, rather than those with the most traffic.
Some cities have responded by painting roofs white. In one experiment in New York, white roofs were found to be up to 24°C cooler than black roofs on summer afternoons.

However, engineer Marco Bellini argues that white roofs alone are not enough. He believes that cities should prioritise “green corridors” — lines of trees and parks — that allow cooler air to flow through streets.
Not every solution has been successful. In one Spanish city, artificial grass was installed in public squares, but it actually became hotter than the asphalt it replaced and was later removed.
Experts predict that, by 2050, more than two-thirds of the world's population will live in cities, making heat one of the most important urban health issues of the century.
